1 · Physical Properties

The easiest way to group elements is by comparing physical properties. Test each property yourself in the mini-labs below — exactly what Activities 3.1 – 3.7 of the book do with iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium, sodium, lead and zinc samples.

3.1.2 · Non-metals

There are far fewer non-metals than metals. Examples: carbon, sulphur, iodine, oxygen, hydrogen. They are either solids or gases — except bromine, which is a liquid.

  • →Coal / graphite and sulphur are soft, dull solids
  • →They are not malleable, not ductile — they break into powder
  • →Poor conductors of heat & electricity
  • →Not sonorous

Section 3.2

2 · Chemical Properties of Metals

Elements are more clearly classified as metals or non-metals on the basis of their chemical properties. Work through the four labs — air, water, acids and salt solutions — and watch every reaction from Sections 3.2.1 – 3.2.4 happen live.

🔥 Burn a metal in air

Hold a sample with tongs over a flame (Activity 3.9). Almost all metals combine with oxygen to give metal oxides.

Metal + Oxygen → Metal oxide

Pick a metal sample

Sodium Magnesium Aluminium Zinc Iron filings Copper Gold

Select a metal on the left, then watch the flame, surface and product.

⚛️ Amphoteric oxides

Most metal oxides are basic. But Al₂O₃ and ZnO react with both acids and bases to give salt + water — they are amphoteric oxides.

with Acid (HCl) with Base (NaOH)

🫧 Soluble oxides → alkalis

Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but Na₂O and K₂O dissolve to form alkalis:

Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)
K₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq)

Do You Know? — Anodising: a process of forming a thick oxide layer of aluminium. A clean Al article is made the anode and electrolysed with dilute H₂SO₄; oxygen evolved at the anode reacts with Al to make a thicker protective oxide layer, which can be dyed for an attractive finish.

💧 React metals with water

Metals react with water to give a metal oxide + hydrogen gas. Soluble oxides further form metal hydroxides. But all metals don't react!

Metal + Water → Metal oxide + Hydrogen
Metal oxide + Water → Metal hydroxide

1 · Pick a metal

Potassium Sodium Calcium Magnesium Aluminium Iron Lead Gold

2 · Choose conditions

❄️ Cold water ♨️ Hot water ☁️ Steam

beaker

Watch: fire on water (K/Na), floating (Ca/Mg), H₂ bubbles, or nothing at all.

Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil? K and Na react so vigorously with oxygen that they catch fire if kept in the open — kerosene keeps air away.

From the book — Fig. 3.3: Action of steam on a metal (glass wool + water, burnt metal, H₂ collected over water).

🧪 React metals with dilute acid

Metals react with dilute acids to give a salt + hydrogen gas (Activity 3.11 — thermometers dipped in test tubes!).

Metal + Dilute acid → Salt + Hydrogen

Drop a metal into dilute HCl

Magnesium Aluminium Zinc Iron Copper

Temp. rise →
0°C
dilute HCl

Bubble rate + heat tell you the reactivity order: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe … and Cu does nothing.

The nitric acid exception: H₂ gas is NOT evolved when a metal reacts with HNO₃, because HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent — it oxidises the H₂ to water and is itself reduced to nitrogen oxides (N₂O, NO, NO₂).
Exception within the exception: Mg and Mn react with very dilute HNO₃ to evolve H₂.

Do You Know? — Aqua regia (Latin: 'royal water') is a freshly prepared mixture of 3 : 1 concentrated HCl : concentrated HNO₃. It is one of the few reagents that can dissolve gold and platinum, though neither acid can do so alone. Highly corrosive, fuming liquid!

3 · How do Metals & Non-Metals React?

Noble gases have a completely filled valence shell and are almost unreactive. Every element reacts to attain this stable state — metals lose electrons (→ cations) and non-metals gain electrons (→ anions). Build your own ionic compound below!

⚛️ Ionic Bond Builder

💡 Compounds formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal are ionic / electrovalent compounds. They exist as aggregates of oppositely charged ions, not molecules.

3.3.1 · Properties of Ionic Compounds (Activity 3.13)

🧱

Physical nature

Hard, brittle solids — strong electrostatic forces hold the oppositely charged ions; they break into pieces under pressure.

🌡️

High melting & boiling points

Considerable energy is needed to break the strong inter-ionic attraction.

Table 3.4 (K): NaCl m.p. 1074, b.p. 1686 · CaO m.p. 2850, b.p. 3120 · MgCl₂ 981/1685
💧

Solubility

Generally soluble in water but insoluble in kerosene, petrol (Activity 3.13).

🔌

Conduction

Conduct electricity in molten state and in solution (ions move freely) — but NOT as solids (rigid structure, ions can't move).

Section 3.4

4 · Occurrence & Extraction of Metals

The earth's crust is the major source of metals; seawater holds soluble salts like NaCl and MgCl₂. How a metal is extracted depends on where it sits in the reactivity series — run the full journey below.

⛰️

Mineral

The elements or compounds that occur naturally in the earth's crust.

⛏️

Ore

A mineral with a very high percentage of metal, from which the metal can be profitably extracted.

🪨

Gangue

Impurities like soil and sand contaminating the mined ore — removed by enrichment before extraction.

From the book — Fig. 3.9: Activity series and related metallurgy.

🗺️ Click a reactivity zone

Metals are grouped into three categories — each uses a different extraction technique. The zones match Fig. 3.9.

Select a zone to see how those metals occur and how they're extracted…

🚂 The Extraction Journey

Pick any metal and follow the steps from its ore to the refined metal (Fig. 3.10). Every step shows its chemical equation.

Mercury (HgS) Copper (Cu₂S) Zinc (ZnS / ZnCO₃) Iron (Fe₂O₃) Sodium (NaCl) Aluminium (Al₂O₃)

🔥 Roasting

Sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating strongly in excess of air.

2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) —Heat→ 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g)

Used for sulphide ores — also removes volatile impurities.

🏺 Calcination

Carbonate ores are changed into oxides by heating strongly in limited air.

ZnCO₃(s) —Heat→ ZnO(s) + CO₂(g)

Used for carbonate ores — drives off CO₂ and moisture.

⚡ The Thermit Reaction

Displacement reactions between metal oxides and highly reactive metals are highly exothermic — so much heat that the metal comes out in the molten state! Iron(III) oxide + aluminium is used to join railway tracks or cracked machine parts.

Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → 2Fe(l) + Al₂O₃(s) + Heat

Also: 3MnO₂ + 4Al → 3Mn + 2Al₂O₃ + Heat (used to extract manganese)

From the book — Fig. 3.11: Thermit process for joining railway tracks.

🔋 3.4.5 · Extracting metals at the TOP of the series — Electrolytic reduction

Carbon cannot reduce the oxides of Na, Mg, Ca, Al — these metals have more affinity for oxygen than carbon. So they are obtained by electrolysis of their molten chlorides: metal is deposited at the cathode (−), chlorine is liberated at the anode (+).

At cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
At anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
Section 3.4.6

🎬 Electrolytic Refining of Copper — the video

The electrolyte is a solution of acidified copper sulphate. The anode is impure copper, the cathode is a strip of pure copper. On passing current, pure copper deposits on the cathode — watch the anode shrink, the cathode grow, and anode mud accumulate at the bottom. Scrub the timeline to jump to any moment.

startanode dissolving…cathode growing…anode mud settlesend
0%
Anode (impure Cu): copper dissolves into the electrolyte as Cu²⁺; soluble impurities go into solution; insoluble ones settle as anode mud.
Cathode (pure Cu strip): an equivalent amount of pure copper from the electrolyte is deposited on it.
Many metals — Cu, Zn, Sn, Ni, Ag, Au — are refined this way. Question 8 of the exercise asks you to generalise this for any metal M!

Book — Fig. 3.12

✏️ Exam tip: remember the trio — anode = impure metal, cathode = thin strip of pure metal, electrolyte = solution of the metal salt. This exact diagram is asked in boards almost every year.

From the book — Fig. 3.13: Investigating the conditions under which iron rusts. In tube A, both air and water are present; in tube B there is no air dissolved in the water; in tube C the air is dry.

Conclusion: Iron rusts only when both air and water are present — prevention works by keeping either one away from the metal surface.

3.5.1 · Preventing Corrosion

🎨

Painting

🛢️

Oiling & greasing

🛡️

Galvanising (Zn coat)

✨

Chrome plating

🧪

Anodising

🔗

Making alloys

Galvanisation = coating steel/iron with a thin layer of zinc. The article stays protected even if the zinc coating breaks — zinc is more reactive than iron and gets oxidised (sacrificially) in place of it.

🔗 Alloy Mixer

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal + non-metal. Pick a famous alloy to see its recipe, properties and uses.

Steel Stainless steel Brass Bronze Solder 22-carat gold Amalgam

Select an alloy →

Composition

📏 Pure gold (24 carat) is very soft — 22 carat = 22 parts gold + 2 parts Cu/Ag.

⚡ Alloys have lower electrical conductivity and melting point than pure metals — brass & bronze conduct poorly, but copper is used in circuits. An alloy with mercury is an amalgam.

The iron pillar at Delhi

🏛️ The wonder of ancient Indian metallurgy

The iron pillar near the Qutub Minar in Delhi was built more than 1600 years ago by the iron workers of India, who developed a process that prevented iron from rusting. Its rust resistance has been examined by scientists from all over the world. The pillar is 8 m high and weighs about 6 tonnes (6000 kg).

✅ What you have learnt

Elements are classified as metals and non-metals. Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat & electricity, and sonorous; solids at room temperature except mercury.
Metals form positive ions by losing electrons; non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons when they react with metals.
Metal oxides are generally basic; Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric. Non-metal oxides are acidic or neutral.
Different metals have different reactivities with water and dilute acids. Metals above hydrogen in the activity series displace H₂ from dilute acids.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution — the basis of the activity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au).
Ionic/electrovalent compounds are formed by electron transfer; they are hard, high-melting, water-soluble, and conduct in the molten/aqueous state.
Extraction of metals from ores and their refining is called metallurgy: low reactivity → heating alone; middle → roasting/calcination then reduction with carbon; top → electrolytic reduction.
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of metals (or metal + non-metal). Corrosion (e.g. rusting of iron) needs both air and moisture; prevented by painting, galvanising, alloying etc.
